message.content:
**Short answer:**  
- **Typical difference:** 9 hours (Berlin +9 hours ahead of Los Angeles).  
- **During the brief “transition” periods** (when one side has switched to DST and the other hasn’t yet), the gap can be **8 or 10 hours**.

---

### Why it can change

| Period | Los Angeles (PT) | Berlin (CET/CEST) | Difference |
|--------|------------------|-------------------|------------|
| **Standard time** (early Nov – mid‑Mar) | UTC‑8 | UTC+1 | +9 h |
| **After LA switches to DST** (mid‑Mar – late‑Mar) | UTC‑7 | UTC+1 | +8 h |
| **After Berlin switches to DST** (late‑Mar – early Oct) | UTC‑7 | UTC+2 | +9 h |
| **After Berlin ends DST** (late‑Oct – early Nov) | UTC‑7 | UTC+1 | +8 h |
| **After LA ends DST** (early Nov – end Dec) | UTC‑8 | UTC+1 | +9 h |

*The exact dates shift each year because the U.S. and EU change clocks on different Sundays.*

---

### Practical tip

If you’re scheduling across time zones:

1. **Use a reliable time‑zone converter** (e.g., [timeanddate.com](https://www.timeanddate.com/worldclock/converter.html) or the built‑in “World Clock” feature on most smartphones).
2. **Double‑check the date**—especially if it falls within the last two weeks of March or the last week of October/first week of November.
3. **Add a buffer** (e.g., 15–30 minutes) when planning critical meetings to account for any confusion over DST transitions.

---

#### Quick reference (2026)

| Date range | LA | Berlin | Gap |
|------------|----|--------|-----|
| Jan – mid‑Mar | UTC‑8 | UTC+1 | +9 h |
| mid‑Mar – late‑Mar | UTC‑7 | UTC+1 | +8 h |
| late‑Mar – early Oct | UTC‑7 | UTC+2 | +9 h |
| early Oct – late‑Oct | UTC‑7 | UTC+1 | +8 h |
| late‑Oct – early Nov | UTC‑8 | UTC+1 | +9 h |

*(These dates are based on the 2026 calendar; always verify for the specific year.)*

---

**Bottom line:** For most of the year, Berlin is **9 hours ahead** of Los Angeles. Just remember the short windows around the DST change‑over dates when the difference temporarily shifts to 8 or 10 hours.
